quotes.text: They were the best damn live band that ever walked the planet, and nobody really gives them their due for it. They sounded so much better than everyone else because they always were so much better than everyone else.

While Freddie was their lead singer, there was never a band so consistently brilliant live as Queen. Every single time they went out, they blew everyone's socks off. There was no slow decline, no loss of finesse or intensity, no sloppiness or mediocrity creeping in over the years – Freddie's last tour was as strong as all the rest had been, and that's in spite of health problems beginning to raise their ugly head.
No band ever has maintained that level of superb quality of performance in their career start to finish.

Queen sort of stumbled into arena rock when their popularity reached overflow conditions and Brian May took notice of how the crowds expressed a fervent wish to participate in the experience. He came up with a nifty little two-step-clap-and-a-pause beat designed to further encourage concert-goers to join in the fun.
Freddie Mercury's a cappella vocal in the verses is strong and sassy as he sings of three "buddies," each at a different stage of life.

It takes about ten seconds to figure out that "We Are the Champions" is a Freddie Mercury composition with its carefully composed piano pattern and melodic movement. From a musical perspective, it's a brilliant piece, featuring verses that move from minor to major as the narrator's spirit lifts, then changing keys entirely for the more confident chorus with its superbly executed harmonies and satisfying musical conclusion.

The most interesting song on the album is probably "My Fairy King," featuring Freddie's piano playing and lots of vocal overdubs, since both would become trademarks of Queen's songwriting throughout their career. It was written and built-up in the studio, unlike most of the other tracks, which were just songs the band had been performing live.
Queen's debut album is the sound of a young band still trying to find itself.
Brian's compositions have more of a traditional rock feel, but they also feature early examples of his unique guitar technique, in which he makes his homemade Red Special sound like an orchestra.
Freddie's songs are more progressive and all flow into one another, with a musical complexity that foreshadowed the band's future masterpieces.
After the mixed critical reaction to Queen II, the band waved goodbye to their prog influences and began recording songs with (what we now know as) the classic Queen sound.
This album showcased experimentation with a variety of musical genres, including heavy metal, vaudeville, piano ballad, ragtime, and Caribbean.
It represents the pinnacle of the band's musical creativity, with diverse genres ranging from music-hall, Dixieland jazz, skiffle, proto-metal, prog, to straight-up rock.
Completely self-produced by the band, A Day at the Races shares similar cover-art, a similar title, and similar musical themes with its sister album.
The band also ventured into proto-metal with "Tie Your Mother Down," music-hall with the bouncy "Good Old-Fashioned Lover Boy," and even singing in Japanese with the rousing ballad "Teo Torriatte."
On the whole, News of the World is more of a mainstream record with less complex arrangements, but it remains a landmark album, an arena rock classic.

this disc created a totally cohesive statement from some of the most diverse, often decidedly un-rock 'n' roll elements. What other band could sandwich a crunching ode to autophilia sung by the drummer with a sweet, tender pop song written by the bassist and a folk tune about suspended animation written and sung by the guitarist?

It's an incredible testament to this fearsome foursome (guitarist Brian May, bassist John Deacon, drummer Roger Taylor, and frontman Freddie Mercury), whose individual creative visions combine to make something truly special that has stood the test of time.

this album found Queen on the cusp of punk but still doing things their own way. So while you get songs like the raucous "Sheer Heart Attack," there's also the haunting harmonies dedicated Brian May's deceased cat, jaunty maracas, and the gloriously bluesy material.
This was the first Queen album to contain synthesizers, a concession to the '80s that worked well enough on this disc but would come to haunt them on later forays.
This is one of the more straightforward Queen discs, solidly enjoyable but a little less baroque than their prior outings.
While less ambitious than Opera, it's hard to quibble with the epic tenderness and soaring harmonies and joyous frivolity of its best tracks.

Sheer Heart Attack was a band on the verge of a breakthrough. "Killer Queen" was their first big single, veering away from their hard rock roots and announcing their devotion to meticulous arrangements.
May's guitar provides a crystal-clear tone that is so recognizably his own, while the multitracked harmonies create the embracing tonal ambiance that is signature Queen.

Songs like the chugging, layered "Now I'm Here" and the gorgeously swaying "In The Lap Of The Gods...Revisited" remained concert staples through their career, connecting Queen with their early sound even as they charted new waters.
Sheer Heart Attack is a little piecemeal as a record, but it gives a glimpse of the band's ambitions, as they would only stay on the brink for so long.
